label: Cupif-Giannini tree traversal
summary: NIST DADS describes Cupif-Giannini tree traversal as: Visit the leaves of a perfect binary tree with maximum dispersion: the next leaf has the maximum shortest-path distance from the preceding leaf, with less importance given to distance from earlier leaves. Use an n-bit counter for a tree of height n; successive bits choose left or right branches starting at the root. An initial random n-bit key can be XORed with the counter to permute the leaf-visit order.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: CupifGianniniTreeTraversal

label: Hamming distance
summary: NIST DADS describes Hamming distance as: The number of bits that differ between two binary strings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: HammingDistance

label: Schorr-Waite graph marking algorithm
summary: NIST DADS describes Schorr-Waite graph marking algorithm as: Mark all reachable nodes of a directed binary graph by reversing pointers on descent and restoring them on departure. Nodes must have out-degree at most two; another graph may first be represented as a binary graph. The procedure uses a few extra bits per node and a few work pointers.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: SchorrWaiteGraphMarking

label: adjacency-matrix representation
summary: NIST DADS describes adjacency-matrix representation as: Represent a directed graph by a square matrix with one row and column per vertex. An entry is one when there is an edge from its row vertex to its column vertex, and zero otherwise. A weighted graph may instead use edge weights. For an undirected graph, symmetric entries or an upper triangular matrix may be used.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adjacencyMatrixRep

label: binary GCD
summary: NIST DADS describes binary GCD as: Compute the greatest common divisor of two integers expressed in binary.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryGCD

label: binary tree representation of trees
summary: NIST DADS describes binary tree representation of trees as: Represent a multiway tree as a binary tree: a node's leftmost child becomes its left child, and a child's immediately right sibling becomes that child's right child.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryTreeRepofTree

label: binomial tree
summary: NIST DADS describes binomial tree as: An ordered tree of order k, with k nonnegative, whose root has k children; its ith child is a binomial tree of order k minus i.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binomialtree

label: bisector
summary: NIST DADS describes bisector as: The locus of points equidistant from two given elements under a distance metric.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bisector

label: B+-tree
summary: NIST DADS describes B+-tree as: A B-tree in which keys are stored in the leaves.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bplustree

label: circuit value problem
summary: NIST DADS describes circuit value problem as: Given an encoded Boolean circuit, its inputs and a designated output, decide whether that output is true on those inputs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circuitvalue

label: cutting theorem
summary: NIST DADS describes cutting theorem as: For n lines in the plane and a parameter r between one and n, a cutting partitions the plane into disjoint triangles, some possibly unbounded, such that no triangle intersects more than n divided by r of the lines. NIST states that such cuttings exist.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cuttingtherm

label: dual linear program
summary: NIST DADS describes dual linear program as: Every linear program has a corresponding linear program called its dual. For an integer linear program, a solution to the dual of a relaxation can serve as a witness.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: duallinear

label: Euclidean distance
summary: NIST DADS describes Euclidean distance as: The straight-line distance between two points.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: euclidndstnc

label: exponential
summary: NIST DADS describes exponential as: In one sense, a sum of constant multiples of constants raised to the power of the argument. In complexity theory, a measure of computation, usually execution time or memory, bounded by an exponential function of problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: exponential

label: factorial
summary: NIST DADS describes factorial as: For an integer argument greater than one, factorial satisfies the recurrence that its value is the argument times the factorial of the preceding integer. NIST also specifies that zero factorial equals one.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: factorial

label: Fibonacci number
summary: NIST DADS describes Fibonacci number as: A member of a sequence in which each number is the sum of the preceding two. The sequence begins one, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonacciNumber

label: Fisher-Yates shuffle
summary: NIST DADS describes Fisher-Yates shuffle as: Randomly permute a sequence by exchanging each element, in order, with a randomly selected element from its position through the end. NIST reports linear running time and a random-bit requirement proportional to the sequence length times its logarithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fisherYatesShuffle

label: full array
summary: NIST DADS describes full array as: A combinatorial-chemistry term for trying all possible combinations of blocks. NIST explicitly states that this term does not name a data structure.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullArray

label: gamma function
summary: NIST DADS describes gamma function as: NIST reports that gamma at the next argument equals the current argument times gamma at the current argument, and that gamma at one more than a nonnegative integer equals that integer's factorial.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gammaFunction

label: Gray code
summary: NIST DADS describes Gray code as: An ordering of binary numbers in which only one bit changes from one entry to the next. Gray codes for four or more bits are not unique even allowing for permutations or inversions of bits.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graycode

label: hidden Markov model
summary: NIST DADS describes hidden Markov model as: A finite-state-machine variant with states, an output alphabet, transition probabilities, output probabilities and initial-state probabilities. The current state is unobservable; each state produces an output with a specified probability. When the state and output sets are understood, NIST describes the model by its three collections of probabilities.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hiddenMarkovModel

label: Horner's rule
summary: NIST DADS describes Horner's rule as: Evaluate a polynomial at a point using repeated multiplication and addition rather than separately raising the argument to powers, multiplying by coefficients and accumulating the results.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hornersrule

label: huge sparse array
summary: NIST DADS describes huge sparse array as: Store unique-key items using an item array large enough for the items and an uninitialized location array covering the much larger key range. Insertion records the next item position in the location array. Lookup validates the stored position against the number of inserted items and checks the item's key. Keys must be unique; duplicate keys require collision resolution. NIST reports linear total insertion and listing time, and constant lookup time, assuming constant-time allocation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hugeSparseArray

label: hypergraph
summary: NIST DADS describes hypergraph as: A graph whose undirected hyperedges connect two or more vertices. It consists of a vertex set and a collection of hyperedges, each of which is a set of vertices.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hypergraph

label: HyperLogLog
summary: NIST DADS describes HyperLogLog as: Estimate the number of distinct items by hashing each item, using initial hash bits to select a counter and updating that counter using the remaining hash bits. After processing the items, the procedure uses a harmonic mean derived from leading-zero counts to form the estimate.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hyperloglog

label: inclusion-exclusion principle
summary: NIST DADS describes inclusion-exclusion principle as: A rule for computing the probability of exactly a specified number of occurrences among a collection of events.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inclusion

label: inverse Ackermann function
summary: NIST DADS describes inverse Ackermann function as: A two-parameter function whose value grows very slowly. NIST cautions that it is not strictly the inverse of Ackermann's function; its growth is described as slow in comparison with Ackermann's rapid growth.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inverseAckermann

label: jump list
summary: NIST DADS describes jump list as: A sorted doubly linked list with two additional levels of links spanning geometrically increasing distances.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jumpList

label: knapsack problem
summary: NIST DADS describes knapsack problem as: Given items with different values and volumes, find the most valuable set that fits a knapsack of fixed volume. Each item is either taken or not taken. NIST also calls this the zero-one or binary knapsack problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: knapsackProblem

label: kth order Fibonacci numbers
summary: NIST DADS describes kth order Fibonacci numbers as: A sequence in which each number is the sum of the k preceding numbers. The usual Fibonacci numbers are the case k equals two.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kthOrderFibonacci

label: kth shortest path
summary: NIST DADS describes kth shortest path as: Find the kth shortest path from one graph vertex to another. Variants may require edge-disjoint or vertex-disjoint paths; shortest may mean fewest edges or least total weight.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kthShortestPath

label: layered graph
summary: NIST DADS describes layered graph as: A connected graph whose vertices are partitioned into layers. Edges have nonnegative integer weights and connect only vertices in successive layers. Its width is the largest number of vertices in any layer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: layeredgraph

label: linear
summary: NIST DADS describes linear as: In one sense, a constant times the argument plus a constant. In complexity theory, a measure of computation, usually execution time or memory, bounded by a linear function of problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linear

label: linear congruential generator
summary: NIST DADS describes linear congruential generator as: A class of pseudorandom number generators that compute each number from the current one using a linear congruence. The current number is multiplied by a constant, another constant is added, and the result is reduced modulo a modulus; NIST requires the multiplier and modulus to be relatively prime.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearCongruentGen

label: linear hashing
summary: NIST DADS describes linear hashing as: A dynamic hash table that grows one slot at a time. Its family of hash functions has ranges that double between successive functions. A split pointer tracks slots already split; splitting a slot and advancing the pointer maintains the load factor. After the pointer reaches the end, the ranges double and the pointer starts over.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearHashing

label: linear probing sort
summary: NIST DADS describes linear probing sort as: Distribute items into a larger array according to interpolation of their keys, putting collisions into the next empty location, then pack the items into an array of the original size. Extra space at the end handles overflow, but NIST states that the sort may fail if that overflow space is exceeded.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearProbingSort

label: linear program
summary: NIST DADS describes linear program as: An optimization problem that minimizes a vector-dot-product objective subject to componentwise linear inequalities and nonnegative decision variables.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearProgramming

label: L_m distance
summary: NIST DADS describes L_m distance as: A generalized distance between two points, also called Minkowski distance. NIST identifies Euclidean distance with the member indexed by two and rectilinear or Manhattan distance with the member indexed by one.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lmdistance

label: Lotka's law
summary: NIST DADS describes Lotka's law as: A power law relating the number of authors to their number of contributions, often nearly an inverse-square law.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lotkaslaw

label: matrix multiplication
summary: NIST DADS describes matrix multiplication as: A binary operation on two matrices, requiring the first matrix's column count to equal the second matrix's row count. The product has the first matrix's row count and the second matrix's column count.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matrixMultiply

label: merge
summary: NIST DADS describes merge as: Combine two or more sorted sequences of data into a single sorted sequence.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: merge

label: Miller-Rabin
summary: NIST DADS describes Miller-Rabin as: A heuristic primality test that repeatedly checks pseudoprimality to randomly chosen bases and whether square roots of one modulo the tested number are trivial. Some composite numbers may be incorrectly judged prime.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: millerRabin

label: moderately exponential
summary: NIST DADS describes moderately exponential as: Growth in a measure of computation, usually execution time or memory, that exceeds every polynomial but is slower than every exponential with base greater than one.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: moderatexpon

label: multiplication method
summary: NIST DADS describes multiplication method as: A hash function based on multiplying a key by an irrational number between zero and one, or an approximation to it. The modulo-one operation removes the integer part of that product.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiplicationMethod

label: NC many-one reducibility
summary: NIST DADS describes NC many-one reducibility as: One language is NC many-one reducible to another when a function in FNC maps an input into the second language if and only if that input belongs to the first.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nCmanyone

label: optimal merge
summary: NIST DADS describes optimal merge as: Merge sorted sequences of different lengths into one output while minimizing reads, merging only two sequences at a time. At each step merge the two shortest sequences and repeat until one remains.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimalMerge

label: parallel prefix computation
summary: NIST DADS describes parallel prefix computation as: Compute an associative function over every prefix of an array in parallel. For an n-element array, NIST reports Θ(n) processors and Θ(log n) time. Parallel iterations must read the old array values before overwriting them; input values can first be copied to a result array in parallel.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: parallelPrefix

label: partition
summary: NIST DADS describes partition as: In one sense, divide a set into nonempty disjoint subsets that together cover the original set. In another, rearrange array elements into two or more groups, typically separating values below and above a chosen value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partition

label: Patricia tree
summary: NIST DADS describes Patricia tree as: A compact trie representation that merges a node that is an only child with its parent. NIST's note uses radix tree for a binary Patricia tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: patriciatree

label: P-complete
summary: NIST DADS describes P-complete as: Under NC reducibility, a language is P-complete if it belongs to P and is P-hard.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pcomplete

label: perfect k-ary tree
summary: NIST DADS describes perfect k-ary tree as: A k-ary tree with all leaf nodes at the same depth and all internal nodes of degree k. NIST notes that authors differ in their terminology.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfectKaryTree

label: polyhedron
summary: NIST DADS describes polyhedron as: The solution set of a finite system of linear inequalities on real-valued variables.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polyhedron

label: polylogarithmic
summary: NIST DADS describes polylogarithmic as: In one sense, a sum of constant multiples of powers of a logarithm of the argument. In complexity theory, a measure of computation bounded by a polylogarithmic function of problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polylogarith

label: polynomial
summary: NIST DADS describes polynomial as: In one sense, a sum of constant multiples of powers of the argument. In complexity theory, a measure of computation bounded by a polynomial function of problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomial

label: quadtree
summary: NIST DADS describes quadtree as: A tree in which each node is split along every dimension. NIST notes that the original two-dimensional picture representation gave each node four children.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadtree

label: quadtree complexity theorem
summary: NIST DADS describes quadtree complexity theorem as: For quadtree representations of simple polygons with nonintersecting edges and no holes, NIST reports that node count is proportional to perimeter when the image-resolution term in its bound is negligible. It also reports an analogous three-dimensional statement with surface area replacing perimeter.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadtreecplx

label: select kth element
summary: NIST DADS describes select kth element as: Find the kth smallest element of a set. NIST describes modified distribution sort and select-and-partition as two approaches and also calls this the selection problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectkth

label: set cover
summary: NIST DADS describes set cover as: A collection of sets whose union covers the members of the full collection's union. The set-cover problem seeks a collection of minimum size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: setcover

label: spiral storage
summary: NIST DADS describes spiral storage as: A dynamic hash table that grows a few slots at a time and uses a hash function with range from zero inclusive to one exclusive.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spiralStorage

label: tabulation hashing
summary: NIST DADS describes tabulation hashing as: Compute a hash value by XORing values drawn from tables indexed by the input characters.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tabulationHashing

label: taco sort
summary: NIST DADS describes taco sort as: A deliberately inefficient sorting algorithm that repeatedly changes a random item by a random amount until a sorted permutation occurs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tacoSort

label: Θ
summary: NIST DADS describes Θ as: An asymptotically tight execution-resource bound: for all sufficiently large problem sizes, a function lies between two fixed positive constant multiples of the comparison function. The constants and size threshold must not depend on problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: theta

label: towers of Hanoi
summary: NIST DADS describes towers of Hanoi as: Given three posts and disks of decreasing sizes, move the disks from one post to another one at a time without placing a larger disk on a smaller disk.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: towersOfHanoi

label: twisted tabulation hashing
summary: NIST DADS describes twisted tabulation hashing as: A tabulation-hashing variant in which a table is indexed by the XOR of the last character and a twister value obtained from the rest of the string. NIST notes that the first character may instead be treated specially.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twistedTabulationHashing

label: 2-choice hashing
summary: NIST DADS describes 2-choice hashing as: A hash-table variant that hashes each key with two hash functions and places it at the position containing fewer colliding keys. A collision-resolution scheme is needed unless keys are kept in buckets.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twoChoiceHashing

label: 2-left hashing
summary: NIST DADS describes 2-left hashing as: A dictionary implemented with two equal-sized hash tables and two different hash functions. Put a new key in the second table only when its candidate position has fewer colliding keys than the first table's position; ties go to the first table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twoLeftHashing

label: unbounded knapsack problem
summary: NIST DADS describes unbounded knapsack problem as: Given item types with different values and volumes, find the most valuable set that fits a fixed-volume knapsack, with no bound on the count of each type. NIST describes this as an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: unboundedKnapsack

label: Zipf's law
summary: NIST DADS describes Zipf's law as: A distribution of word or item occurrence probabilities in which a few items occur very often and many occur rarely.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: zipfslaw

label: Benford's law
summary: NIST DADS reports Benford's law as follows: On a wide variety of statistical data, the probability that the first digit is d is the base-ten logarithm of one plus the reciprocal of d.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: benfordslaw

label: Kraft's inequality
summary: NIST DADS states Kraft's inequality for a binary tree: Sum, over all its leaves, two raised to the negative depth of each leaf. That sum is at most one.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kraftsinqlty

label: linear product
summary: NIST DADS describes a linear product of two vectors using suitable operations ⊗ and ⊕. For each output index k from zero through m+n, combine under ⊕ the terms X[i] ⊗ Y[j] whose indices satisfy i+j=k. The printed result has components Z[0] through Z[m+n].

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearprodct

label: slope selection
summary: Katz and Sharir's original publication abstract defines slope selection as: Given n points in the plane and an integer k, find the pair of points whose connecting line has the kth smallest slope.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: slopeselectn
Katz and Sharir: Optimal Slope Selection via Expanders — institutional publication abstract

label: Stirling's approximation
summary: NIST DADS gives Stirling's approximation for large values of n: n! ≈ (n/e)^n * sqrt(2*n*pi). Here ^ denotes exponentiation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stirlingsApproximation

label: Stirling's formula
summary: NIST DADS gives the following Stirling bounds for large values of n. Set S = (n/e)^n * sqrt(2*n*pi); then S < n! < S * (1 + 1/(12*n-1)). Here ^ denotes exponentiation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stirlingsFormula

label: bucket array
summary: NIST DADS describes bucket array as: A dictionary implementation using an array indexed by the keys of the dictionary items.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketarray

label: cube root
summary: NIST DADS describes cube root as: A manual, long-hand method of extracting cube roots, described by NIST DADS as similar to long-hand division or its manual square-root method. This scoped description does not reproduce the numerical worked example.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cubeRoot

label: square root
summary: NIST DADS describes square root as: A manual, long-hand method of extracting square roots, described by NIST DADS as similar to long-hand division. This scoped description does not reproduce the numerical worked example.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: squareRoot

label: Big Omega (asymptotic lower bound)
summary: NIST DADS describes Big Omega (asymptotic lower bound) as: An asymptotic lower bound in which, beyond some fixed input size, a function is at least a positive constant multiple of the comparison function. Both constants are fixed independently of input size. NIST distinguishes this all-sufficiently-large-inputs definition from a weaker traditional definition requiring only an unbounded sequence of such inputs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: omegaCapital

label: R+-tree
summary: NIST DADS describes R+-tree as: A height-balanced spatial access method that splits space into hierarchically nested boxes and indexes an object in each box intersecting it.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rplustree

label: R*-tree
summary: NIST DADS describes R*-tree as: A height-balanced spatial access method with hierarchically nested, possibly overlapping boxes. NIST describes it as similar to an R-tree but reinserting entries on overflow rather than splitting.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rstartree

label: shortest path
summary: NIST DADS describes shortest path as: The single-pair shortest-path problem seeks the shortest-path weight or distance between graph vertices, using measures such as edge count or total edge weight. NIST distinguishes this value problem from reconstructing the route itself, which requires an algorithm modification.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestpath
